This page contains lecture notes, exercises, and supplementary material for
*Living in the IT Era*, prepared primarily for the first-year BS Biology
students whom I teach. The course is not intended to turn students into
computer technicians or make them memorise catalogues of devices, inventors,
and fashionable technologies. Its purpose is to provide enough working
knowledge to make better decisions about computers, internet services,
software, privacy, security, online conduct, AI, and other technologies that
students encounter in ordinary life and scientific work.

Much of the subject will already be familiar in fragments. A student may know
one part from using a phone, another from connecting to Wi-Fi, and another from
hearing about online scams or AI. The course brings those pieces together,
fills important gaps, and explains how they are related. Examples are drawn
whenever practicable from biology, health, research, and Philippine digital
life.

The module follows the broad general-education scope described for *Living in
the IT Era* in [CHED Memorandum Order No. 20, series of
2013](https://ched.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/CMO-No.20-s2013.pdf).
Its ten-chapter plan is a modern interpretation of that scope rather than a
claim that CHED prescribes this exact sequence. The notes will be developed as
the course proceeds and may change in response to students' questions,
suggestions, and practical needs.

## How classes will work

We shall use a **flipped-classroom approach**. Students first encounter the
assigned material by reading the announced pages or sections before class.
Class meetings will provide a bird's-eye view of the chapter and concentrate
on questions, discussion, examples, and practical applications rather than
repeat the notes line by line.

The assigned reading will not usually be terribly long, and students are not
expected to master it before class. They are, however, expected to read the
assigned sections carefully rather than skim only the headings and examples.
They should arrive familiar with the main ideas and ready to say what was
clear, what was confusing, and what deserves further discussion. Reading
before class is part of the course rather than optional preparation for it.

## House rules

1. **Printed notes are available if you need them.** If you do not have
   reliable access to a laptop or mobile device, speak to me after class or
   during consultation hours. You do not need to explain your circumstances;
   I will provide the relevant printed material free of charge.

2. **Attend regularly and arrive on time.** Much of the course depends on
   discussion, questions, and guided work that cannot be reconstructed fully
   from the notes. The notes are a guide rather than a transcript, and the
   examples or pace may change. Any change affecting examinable material will
   be announced clearly.

3. **Complete the announced reading before class.** Unlike the advance reading
   for MMW, the MST reading should not be treated as a quick skim. Read the
   assigned sections carefully from beginning to end. If you encounter an
   unfamiliar term, make a brief effort to look it up using a search engine or
   dependable reference. This does not require a full research project; the
   aim is simply to understand enough to follow the discussion and identify
   what still needs explanation. Bring those questions, examples from your own
   experience, and claims that you would like the class to examine.

4. **Participate and ask for help.** Questions are welcome in class, by email,
   and during consultation hours. You will not be judged if a technical idea
   is difficult or unfamiliar. Ask classmates, compare notes, and
   speak to me when something remains unclear.

   ::: {.callout-note title="Language in our classroom"}
   The notes use British English. The differences between British and American
   English are relatively subtle in this course, apart from some spelling
   conventions and a few terms, so they should not cause difficulty. Either is
   acceptable if your meaning is clear and consistent. English is useful for
   reading technical and biological literature, but it is not a barrier to
   participation. Students may use any dialect of Tagalog or Cebuano, or
   English. If my accent or wording is difficult to follow, tell me; I can
   explain in Taglish whenever practicable.
   :::

5. **Discuss ideas firmly but civilly.** A useful discussion may involve
   disagreement. Address the claim rather than embarrassing the person who
   made it, distinguish evidence from opinion, and be willing to correct or
   revise a position. The same standard applies to communication in class and
   online.

6. **Use devices and generative AI thoughtfully.** A phone or laptop may be a
   legitimate tool for reading, checking a specification, examining a source,
   or recording a question. Use it for the work at hand without distracting
   other people. Generative-AI tools may offer explanations or alternative
   perspectives, but fluent answers can still be wrong. Check important
   claims against the notes and dependable sources, and do not use AI during a
   graded assessment unless I have expressly permitted it.

7. **Protect other people's information.** Do not share a classmate's personal
   details, messages, photographs, recordings, account information, or
   screenshots without permission. Use fictitious or properly anonymised data
   when an activity does not require real personal information.

8. **Help improve the course.** Please point out factual errors, unclear
   explanations, broken links, and practical topics that the notes have
   overlooked. Correct mistakes respectfully. The notes are being developed
   alongside the course, and well-founded student feedback may shape later
   versions.
